Nodes B, D, and F are selected in the accent color with values 5, 4, and 1; applying the function doubles each to 10, 8, and 2, while the unselected nodes keep 3, 2, and 6." width="100%"} For every node in the current selection that already has the attribute `node_attr=`, calls `func=` with the current value and writes the return value back to the same attribute, modifying the graph in place. Selected nodes that lack the attribute are skipped (the function is not called for them, and the attribute is not created). Unselected nodes are never touched, and the selection itself is left unchanged. Where `set_node_attrs_ws()` writes a fixed value, this method derives the new value from the old one, which makes it a good fit for: - scaling, discounting, or clipping numeric values for a subset of nodes - normalizing or recoding values (e.g., `str.upper`, mapping codes to names) - applying a correction only to nodes matched by a selection If nothing is selected, the call does nothing. Updates are applied node by node, so if `func=` raises an exception partway through, nodes processed earlier keep their new values. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [node_attr]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [str]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Name of the existing attribute to transform (e.g., `"score"`). The result is written back under the same name; to keep the original, copy it to a new attribute first with `set_node_attrs()`. Selected nodes without this attribute are skipped. [func]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Callable]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : A callable taking one argument, the node's current value for `node_attr=`, and returning the new value. It is called once per selected node that has the attribute. It receives only the value (not the node ID), so the transformation must depend on the value alone. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [Graph]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Self for method chaining. ::: ## Examples {.doc-examples} The function receives each selected node's current value and returns the replacement. Here `score` is doubled for `A` and `B`, while `C` was never selected and keeps its original score of `30`: ::: {#84f64b86 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ( ec.Graph() .add_nodes({"A": {"score": 10}, "B": {"score": 20}, "C": {"score": 30}}) ) id_a = graph.get_id_from_label("A") id_b = graph.get_id_from_label("B") ( graph .select_nodes_by_id([id_a, id_b]) .mutate_node_attrs_ws("score", lambda x: x * 2) ) graph.get_node_attrs("score") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` {2: 40, 3: 30, 1: 20} ``` ::: ::: Combining this with `select_nodes()` applies the transformation only to nodes matching a condition (here, discounting prices above `100` by 10%): ::: {#ebbafda0 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph = ( ec.Graph() .add_nodes({"A": {"price": 80}, "B": {"price": 120}, "C": {"price": 150}}) ) ( graph .select_nodes(lambda n: n.attributes.get("price", 0) > 100) .mutate_node_attrs_ws("price", lambda p: p * 0.9) ) graph.get_node_attrs("price") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` {2: 108.0, 3: 135.0, 1: 80} ``` ::: ::: Selected nodes that don't have the attribute are skipped rather than raising an error. Below, all nodes are selected but only `A` has a `name`, so it alone is changed and no `name` is added to `B`: ::: {#70ff308a .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph = ( ec.Graph() .add_node(label="A", name="alice") .add_node(label="B") .select_nodes(lambda n: True) .mutate_node_attrs_ws("name", str.title) ) graph.get_node_attrs("name") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` {1: 'Alice'} ``` ::: :::
